sections.h2: Who keeps the land records for Sandusky County, and how do I reach them?
sections.html:
The Sandusky County Recorder keeps them, from Room 143 of the building at 100 N. Park Ave. in Fremont, ZIP 43420. The counter opens at 8:00 AM and closes at 4:30 PM, Monday to Friday. Dial (419) 334-6226 with questions. The county's own description says the first deed went on record on May 16, 1822, so the files span two centuries of Sandusky County ownership.

Staff index every instrument by name and parcel. A title examiner uses that index to trace a chain of owners and to spot any mortgage or lien still attached. For a copy of something already recorded, the county site asks you to email the recorder's staff.

Fremont is the seat of the county. Bellevue and Clyde are the county's other two cities, and the county site also links Gibsonburg and Woodville. Whichever of them your house sits in, the paper trail ends at the same Fremont counter.

sections.h2: What is the path a Sandusky County deed follows from signing to the record?
sections.html:
Think of it as two counters on one floor. The auditor works first, in Room 109, phone (419) 334-6123. The recorder works second, in Room 143, and only the recorder's stamp puts the deed into the public index.

  • A new deed is drafted with the full legal description, which you can lift from the previous deed shown in the county's online land search.
  • The grantor signs before a notary, or another official Ohio law names for this purpose.
  • The auditor receives the deed along with the state's value statement, collects its fees, and endorses the deed.
  • The recorder takes the endorsed deed, collects the recording charge, and returns the original as you direct.

Closing attorneys and title companies commonly carry the paperwork for you. If you are giving a house to a relative instead of selling it, ask the auditor which exemption form fits before you drive downtown.

sections.h2: Which Ohio statutes decide whether a deed is valid and protected?
sections.html:
Two short sections do most of the work. R.C. 5301.01 says the grantor signs and that the signature is acknowledged before a court judge or clerk, a county auditor or engineer, a notary or a mayor, who then certifies it. A deed without that certificate is not ready to file.

R.C. 5301.25 deals with priority. R.C. 5301.25 sends land instruments to the recorder of the county where the parcel sits. Until a deed is filed there, a later purchaser who paid honestly and knew nothing of it can treat the earlier deed as fraudulent. A seller here should confirm filing after closing.

The same section adds a rule for deeds that follow a survey: the surveyor's name must appear in the deed. Ask your closing agent whether yours needs that wording.

sections.h2: What recording charges does the state schedule set?
sections.html:
The base recording charges come from R.C. 317.32, where every charge is split into two equal halves. A county can layer a preservation surcharge on top, so the counter total may run higher than the statute's figures. Phone the recorder for the posted schedule first.

Fees as printed in R.C. 317.32 (codes.ohio.gov)
ServiceBase feeHousing trust fund fee
Recording and indexing, first two pages$17$17
Every added page (8.5 by 14 inches or part of one)$4$4
Certified copy, each page$1$1
Photocopy made after recording, each page$1$1
Marginal reference in a separate instrument$2$2

The surcharge, capped at five dollars, goes into the county general fund. Payment is due at presentation, though an e-recording submitter may settle by electronic funds transfer afterward.

sections.h2: Who bears the transfer charges when a Sandusky County house sells?
sections.html:
The seller does. The buyer's side files a value statement with the auditor under R.C. 319.202, and the grantor covers the state conveyance fee plus any local tax a county has adopted under Chapter 322.

The state fee in R.C. 319.54(G)(3) is whichever is larger: $1, or ten cents for every $100 of value, with any leftover part of $100 counting as a full unit. R.C. 322.02 lets commissioners adopt a further tax capped at thirty cents per hundred. This page quotes no county total, so ask the Sandusky County Auditor what combined rate applies on your recording date.

The same statute exempts many transfers. A sampling:

  • deeds that only give or release security for a debt
  • corrective deeds that fix one already recorded
  • gifts passing between spouses or from parents to children
  • transfers ordered by a court that are not themselves sales
  • conveyances among the heirs of a single decedent where no money changes hands

An exempt deed still needs a written reason, which the state's DTE 100(EX) form captures.

sections.h2: Does the Sandusky County Recorder accept electronic filings?
sections.html:
It does. A filer signs up with one of four approved providers named on the county's vendor sheet: ePN, CSC eRecording, Simplifile or Hopdox. Lenders, attorneys and title offices typically hold an account with at least one.

Without a title office you can still file by hand. The county's public search link on the recorder page is a useful first stop, since it lets you copy your own legal description and check what is already of record against the parcel.

sections.h2: What do federal figures say about housing in Sandusky County?
sections.html:
The Census Bureau's mid-2025 estimate is 58,655 residents, 0.4 percent under the 2020 base, across 408.25 square miles of dry land. The housing count is 26,530 units holding 24,686 households.

  • Home ownership: 73.4 percent of units are owner-occupied
  • Typical owned home: valued at $160,700
  • Typical rent: $783 a month
  • Typical household income: $62,295
  • Average commute: 20.7 minutes

Because about three in four homes have their owner living inside, most competing listings are owner-occupied houses. The Sandusky River cuts northeast through the county toward Sandusky Bay on Lake Erie, so a parcel near the water deserves a flood-zone check from your title office.

sections.h2: How do Sandusky County property taxes tie into closing?
sections.html:
The county treasurer's site says bills fall due on the third Friday of February and the second Friday of July. Under House Bill 186, the treasurer set August 7, 2026 as the second-half date for the 2025 bills payable in 2026. That date is behind us.

Your closing agent requests the owed amount from the treasurer and holds it back from your proceeds. When a half-year is still open, get the treasurer's payoff number before you commit to a contract. The treasurer's site also links to sheriff sale listings and the county land bank, worth a look if the house passed through a tax foreclosure.

faqs.q: Which office records Sandusky County deeds?
faqs.a: The Sandusky County Recorder, Room 143 at 100 N. Park Ave. in Fremont. It is at 100 N. Park Ave. in Fremont, and the phone is (419) 334-6226.

faqs.q: Which counter comes first, auditor or recorder?
faqs.a: Yes. The auditor reviews the value statement, takes its fees, and endorses the deed. The recorder accepts the instrument after that step.

faqs.q: What is the statutory cost of filing a deed here?
faqs.a: For the first two pages R.C. 317.32 pairs a $17 recording fee with an equal $17 for the state housing trust fund; every page after that carries a $4 and $4 pair. Counties can tack on up to $5 more, so ask the recorder what the full charge is.

faqs.q: Can a deed be recorded electronically in Sandusky County?
faqs.a: Yes, through ePN, CSC eRecording, Simplifile or Hopdox, the four providers on the county's vendor sheet. Title offices and attorneys usually file this way.

faqs.q: What risk comes with leaving a deed unrecorded?
faqs.a: An unrecorded deed loses ground to a later buyer who pays in good faith and has no notice of it, because R.C. 5301.25 labels the earlier instrument fraudulent as to that buyer.
